planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in full sun on lean, fast-draining soil; this species resents wet winter feet far more than it minds cold air.

directions: Native to a handful of gorges and coastal sites on Crete and in adjacent southwest Turkey, this is considered the hardiest true date palm species, with established plants tolerating brief drops to roughly 20-25 degrees F. It forms a dense, usually multi-trunked clump of stiff, silvery-grey, spine-tipped fronds that give it a tough, architectural look distinct from the soft-leaved Phoenix roebelenii. Give it full sun and sharply drained, lean soil; it is highly drought-tolerant once established and is more likely to suffer from soggy clay in a wet Gulf Coast winter than from an isolated freeze. Fruit is small, dry, and seedy and not grown for eating here, but the species is prized strictly as a tough, salt- and wind-tolerant landscape accent.
sources: Riffle and Craft - An Encyclopedia of Cultivated Palms

common_name: Himalayan Mountain Date Palm (Kashmir Date Palm)

planting.note: Transplant in spring into full to partial sun on well-drained soil; young plants benefit from a sheltered microclimate for their first winter or two.

directions: Collected from high elevations across the Himalayan foothills of northeast India, Nepal, and Kashmir, this variety is the cold-hardiest form of an otherwise widespread and variable species, with seed-grown plants from the coldest provenances tolerating short dips into the mid-to-high teens Fahrenheit. It resembles a dwarf, slower-growing Phoenix canariensis, forming a compact rosette of stiff, grey-green, spine-based fronds that stay a manageable size for smaller Gulf Coast landscapes. Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil and expect slow, steady growth with good wind tolerance once established. Because seed strains vary widely in hardiness, buy from a source that specifies high-elevation Kashmir or Himalayan provenance if cold tolerance is the priority.
sources: Rare Palm Seeds - Phoenix loureiroi var. humilis

common_name: Riverbend Cabbage Palm (Cold-Hardy Sabal Palmetto Strain)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun; like all Sabal palms it is slow to establish a root system, so container-grown stock transplants far more reliably than bare-root field-dug trees.

directions: This named seed strain traces to Sabal palmetto trees that survived a severe freeze in the Tifton, Georgia area in the 1980s, and it is grown specifically to push the species' reliable cold hardiness a notch further than typical Florida-sourced seed. Like the straight species it tolerates heat, humidity, drought, flooding, and coastal salt spray with ease, forming the same stately, smooth grey trunk and rounded costapalmate crown prized throughout the Gulf Coast. Expect the usual Sabal palmetto patience test: it spends years building an underground root and bud system before any visible trunk appears above ground. Choose this strain over generic nursery stock specifically for inland or northern-tier zone 8b-9a plantings where an extra few degrees of cold tolerance matters.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun; seedlings are only partially true to the fused-leaflet trait, so buy confirmed, already-leafed-out plants if the distinctive foliage is the goal.

directions: First discovered as a chance mutation in southwest Florida in 1998, this cultivar carries unusually thick, leathery, largely fused leaflets that give each frond a dense, almost solid, textured look rather than the open, finely divided fan of a typical Sabal palmetto. It shares the species' full cold hardiness, tolerating hard freezes into the low teens Fahrenheit once trunked, along with the same outstanding heat, drought, wind, and salt tolerance that makes Sabal palmetto a Gulf Coast landscape staple. Growth is just as slow as the species, gaining only a few inches of visible trunk per year, so treat it as a long-term investment piece rather than a quick screen. Because the fused-leaflet trait is not perfectly fixed from seed, confirm the distinctive foliage is present before buying young, unleafed seedlings.

planting.note: Set out in spring in sun to light shade on moist, well-drained soil; this selection is notably slower growing than typical Sabal minor, so start with the largest container stock available.

directions: Rescued from a construction site near Emerald Isle, North Carolina, this selection of the native dwarf palmetto grows unusually large for the species, eventually reaching up to 7 feet tall and 10 feet wide with broad, exceptionally blue-grey leaves up to 5 feet across. It shares the straight species' excellent cold hardiness, with established clumps surviving temperatures well below 0 degrees F, making it one of the most cold-tolerant fan palms available for Gulf Coast and even mid-Atlantic gardens. The trunk stays mostly underground as with other dwarf palmettos, so the show is entirely in the dramatic blue foliage held on a slowly expanding, stemless clump. Give it a part-shade to full-sun site with reliable moisture and be patient, since it is slower to size up than ordinary green-leaved Sabal minor.

planting.note: Transplant in spring into sun or light shade on moist to dry soil; it adapts to both soggy bottomland and ordinary garden beds once established.

directions: Grown from seed collected near Savannah, Georgia, this selection of the native dwarf palmetto is prized for its strikingly blue-grey fan leaves on a compact, stemless clump that tops out around 3 feet tall. Like all Sabal minor it is extremely cold hardy, with established plants shrugging off temperatures far below anything a Gulf Coast winter delivers, and it tolerates both wet bottomland soils and ordinary dry garden beds with equal ease. Its small mature size makes it a good choice for foundation plantings or understory accents where the larger Sabal palmetto would eventually overwhelm the space. Plant in part shade to full sun and expect slow, trouble-free growth with no feeding or spraying required once it is in the ground.

subcategory: cold-hardy fan palm for temperate gardens

planting.note: Set out in spring in full sun to light shade on well-drained soil; it is equally at home in a large container as in the ground, which makes it easy to overwinter in a protected spot its first year or two.

directions: Selected as a tighter, denser sport of the already-compact 'Vulcano' form, this dwarf European fan palm cultivar holds unusually short leaf stems and densely packed, silvery-backed fronds that stay neat without staking or pruning. It carries the species' excellent cold hardiness, with mature plants tolerating brief drops to around 10 degrees F, making it one of the hardiest clumping fan palms available for Gulf Coast landscaping. Its slow growth and small, tidy mature size suit entryways, patio containers, and mixed borders where a full-size Chamaerops would eventually crowd the space. Plant in full sun on sharply drained soil and water only to establish; like the species it is highly drought-tolerant once rooted in.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in full sun on lean, well-drained soil; seed germination is notoriously slow and erratic, often taking the better part of a year.

directions: Native to rocky, shallow-soil grassland openings in central Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, this rare single-trunked jelly palm grows to a stately 10-20 feet with bright green arching fronds, distinguishing it from the shorter, more silvery-blue common pindo palm. Anecdotal reports from cultivation, including specimens grown unprotected as far north as southern Ohio, suggest it tolerates cold at least as well as Butia odorata. It produces large, sweet-tart edible fruit similar to other jelly palms, used for fresh eating or preserves. Give it full sun and sharp drainage on a lean soil mimicking its native rocky grassland habitat, and expect the same slow but steady growth typical of the genus; it remains rare in cultivation, so source seed or plants from a specialist rare-palm supplier.

subcategory: most cold-hardy fan palm for temperate gardens

planting.note: Set out in spring in full sun to light shade on well-drained soil; young plants benefit from afternoon shade their first year or two in hot Gulf Coast summers.

directions: Grown from seed collected around Kalimpong in the Darjeeling district of northeast India, this seed strain of the windmill palm carries stiffer, more compact leaves than typical Chusan palm stock and is prized by cold-climate growers for the consistent hardiness of plants raised from a single high-altitude seed source. Like other Trachycarpus fortunei strains it tolerates brief drops to around 10 degrees F or slightly below once well established, among the hardiest of all trunk-forming palms. It grows into the same reliable, single-trunked, fan-leaved silhouette as standard windmill palm, reaching 15-25 feet over time, but with a slightly tidier, more uniform crown. Plant in full sun to light shade on well-drained soil and expect steady, trouble-free growth with excellent heat and humidity tolerance in a Gulf Coast setting.

planting.note: Plant rooted offshoots or container stock in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; named cultivars are propagated from offshoots, not seed, to keep the fruiting characteristics true to type.

directions: An old Iraqi cultivar with handsome silvery-green foliage and a tall, clean trunk much like the better-known 'Medjool', Zahidi is grown both as a landscape specimen and for its semi-dry, medium-size dates. As a date palm it tolerates winter cold reasonably well once dormant, but sustained temperatures below about 20 degrees F can damage foliage and crown, and the long, hot, dry summer needed to properly ripen fruit is harder to come by on the humid Gulf Coast than in the desert Southwest where it is commercially grown. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and irrigate deeply but infrequently; good air circulation and dry conditions during fruit ripening help reduce the fungal problems humid climates otherwise encourage. Expect it primarily as a striking architectural palm in zone 9-11 landscapes, with reliable fruit production more likely in drier climates.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension date palm variety trials

planting.note: Plant rooted offshoots in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; this cultivar is propagated vegetatively from offshoots to preserve its soft-date fruiting quality.

directions: Another traditional Iraqi date cultivar, Khadrawy produces smaller, softer, high-moisture dates with a milder sweetness than 'Medjool' and is grown throughout the California and Arizona date belt both for fruit and as a feathery-crowned landscape specimen. Hardiness is similar to other date palm cultivars, with foliage damage likely below roughly 20 degrees F and reliable fruit ripening requiring a long, hot, low-humidity growing season that the Gulf Coast's summer humidity makes difficult to replicate. On the Gulf Coast it is best treated as an ornamental feather palm for a sunny, well-drained site rather than a dependable fruit crop. Water deeply but infrequently once established, since overly wet soil and high humidity around the developing fruit clusters invite rot in a way the arid desert climate it is bred for does not.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension date palm variety trials

planting.note: Plant rooted offshoots in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; as with other named date cultivars, propagate only from offshoots to keep fruit quality true to type.

directions: Halawy, meaning sweet in Arabic, is an Iraqi date cultivar grown for its soft, tender, lightly chewy fruit and for its large, handsome crown, which rivals 'Medjool' in landscape presence. Like other true date palm cultivars it withstands brief winter cold once dormant but can suffer foliage damage below about 20 degrees F, and the long, dry, intensely hot summer needed to ripen a full crop of fruit is more characteristic of the California and Arizona date-growing regions than the humid Gulf Coast. In a Gulf Coast planting it performs reliably as a bold architectural feather palm in full sun on well-drained soil, with fruiting a secondary and less dependable benefit given the region's summer humidity and rainfall. Allow ample room for its ultimate size, since mature date palms form a wide, heavy crown atop a thick trunk over time.
sources: Wikipedia - list of date palm cultivars
University of California Cooperative Extension date palm variety trials
